The author does say that there was an acceptance of slavery in industrial Britain because of a sentiment that carried over from pre-industrial Britain.

But the whole point of bringing up these jerky "certain notables" is to scoff at Drescher's suggestion that Britain had "turned the corner" with its moral sentiments towards slavery.

Eltis is saying, "No, they weren't anti-slavery in their hearts. Look, there were certain notables actually requesting that unemployed people roaming the countryside be enslaved."

choices.text: indicate that the laboring classes provided little support for the abolition of slavery
choices.explanation: At no point is anyone ever blaming laboring classes for not backing the abolition of slavery. And bringing up "certain notables" who said, "Why don't we round up the vagrants and turn them into slaves" has nothing to do with blaming laboring classes for not supporting abolition more.

choices.text: establish that laborers in preindustrial Britain had few civil rights
choices.explanation: Eltis is never trying to establish a big point about whether or not laborers had few vs. many civil rights. He's just trying to establish a big point that Britain was not morally offended by slavery at this point in time.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best states Williams' view of the primary reason for Britain's abolition of the slave trade and the emancipation of slaves in its colonies?

choices.text: British populism appealed to people of varied classes, parties, and religions.
choices.tag: Wrong Point of View / Out of Support Window
choices.explanation: This language relates more to Drescher's moral explanation for the end of slavery. It appeared in the 2nd paragraph, far from our support window in the 1st paragraph.

choices.text: Both capitalists and workers in Britain accepted the moral precepts of abolitionists.
choices.tag: Wrong Point of View / Out of Support Window
choices.explanation: This language relates more to Drescher's moral explanation for the end of slavery. It appeared in the 2nd paragraph, while our support window is the 1st paragraph.

choices.text: Forced labor in the colonies could not produce enough goods to satisfy British consumers.
choices.tag: Wrong Point of View / Out of Support Window
choices.explanation: This language relates more to Eltis's alternative-economic explanation for the end of slavery. It appeared in the 3rd paragraph, while our support window is the 1st paragraph.

choices.text: The operation of colonies based on forced labor was no longer economically advantageous.
choices.explanation: This is the best available match for "primarily for economic reasons / these colonies were an impediment to British economic progress".

choices.text: British workers became convinced that forced labor in the colonies prevented paid workers from receiving higher wages.
choices.tag: Wrong Point of View / Out of Support Window
choices.explanation: This language relates more to Eltis's alternative-economic explanation for the end of slavery. The discussion of higher wages appeared in the 3rd paragraph, while our support window is the 1st paragraph.

questions.prompt: According to Eltis, low wages and Draconian vagrancy laws in Britain in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were intended to

choices.text: protect laborers against unscrupulous employment practices
counter the move to enslave unemployed laborers
ensure a cheap and productive work force
ensure that the work force experienced no unemployment
ensure that products produced in British colonies employing forced labor could compete effectively with those produced in Britain

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the author of the passage views Drescher's presentation of British traditions concerning liberty as

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Drescher's views are discussed in the 2nd paragraph, although in that paragraph he never presents anything about "British traditions of liberty" explicitly.

Instead, that phrase gets used at the beginning of the 3rd paragraph as a reference to what Drescher was talking about in the 2nd paragraph.

When it comes to the passage's central question of *what caused the abolition of slavery in Britain in 1807-1834*, Drescher tries to argue that there may be have been some economic motive, but that there really were also the *humanitarian motives* that Williams thinks were inconsequential.

Drescher shows how a wide swath of people supported antislavery petitions in 1730-1830, and this couldn't have come from economic interest alone.

What is ****the author's**** view concerning Drescher's presentation?

That comes right after a ****Purpose Pivot**** (but, ****yet****, however, recently) in the middle of the 2nd paragraph.

The author says that "Drescher *does* demonstrate that support for antislavery *must have resulted at least in part from widespread literacy and* *****a tradition of political activism******",* but the author does not ultimately find Drescher's causal storyline behind the abolition of British slavery compelling.

When the beginning of the 3rd paragraph refers to Drescher's presentation of British traditions of liberty, the author uses the term *idealizations*, which conveys her attitude that Drescher is being unrealistically charitable.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Because the keywords of the question stem bring us to the 2nd sentence of the 3rd paragraph, where our author is saying that Drescher *idealized* British traditions of liberty, we should look for whichever answer sounds like *idealization*.

choices.text: accurately stated
choices.explanation:
The author thinks that Drescher accurately stated that support for antislavery resulted in part from a tradition of political activism, but she also thinks that Drescher *idealized* the British traditions of liberty.

So "accurately stated" is a little too solid of an endorsement, given the term *idealizations*.

choices.text: somewhat unrealistic
choices.explanation:
This is our best match for our Support Window.

Our author has said, "Sure, you've demonstrated that antislavery support resulted at least in part from a traditional political activism, but you're idealizing the traditions of liberty -- they wouldn't be enough in such a divided country to reach the level of *popular support*, plus the measures were actually proposed by and approved by conservative politicians, who would be unlikely to be on the leading edge of looking out for slaves out of respect for their liberties."

In other words, she thinks the story he's weaving is unrealistic.

choices.text: carefully researched
choices.explanation: There aren't any lines in the 2nd paragraph (or beginning of 3rd) that provide any textual support for the author calling Drescher's presentation of British traditions of liberty as carefully researched.

choices.text: unnecessarily tentative
choices.explanation: If Drescher is ****idealizing**** traditions of liberty, he's going ****too far****. This answer is saying the author felt like he didn't go far enough.

choices.text: superficially convincing
choices.explanation:
This answer would probably apply to the author's view of Drescher's explanation for how abolition came to pass in Britain.

However, this question is specifically about "traditions of liberty", and the best line reference we have for that is that Drescher was ****i****dealizing**** these traditions. That doesn't match *superficially convincing* well.

questions.prompt: The information in the passage suggests that Eltis and Drescher agree that

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Drescher's take on Britain's abolition of the slave trade was a balanced view of "economic considerations + moral reasons".

Drescher is arguing that antislavery was a broadly popular idea, cutting across lines of class, party, and religion. We shouldn't explain the abolition of slavery by citing economic reasons alone.

Eltis rejects Drescher's "idealization of British traditions of liberty" and seemingly pivots back to the, "Nah, it was mainly for economic reasons".

So where do they agree?

Well they definitely that ****part**** of why Britain got rid of slavery was economic. They disagree about how much, but would each conceive it wasn't totally humanitarian / moral.

choices.text: people of all classes in Britain supported the abolition of slavery
choices.explanation:
This might not be tempting on a first pass, but since all the other answers seem to speak directly to the ****disagreement**** between Eltis and Drescher, we might work our way back here through desperation.

Drescher was definitely arguing that people of all classes supported abolition. The 2nd paragraph says:

*Drescher has reconstructed the populist characteristics of British abolitionism, which appears to have cut across lines of class, party, and religion.*

In the last paragraph, Eltis is arguing that the real reason Britain got rid of slavery is that capitalists realized they needed consumers with money to buy sugar / coffee / tobacco.

*Significantly, it was products grown by slaves ... that stimulated new wants* *****at all levels of British society******. ... in an economy that had begun to rely on voluntary labor to satisfy these nonsubsistence needs, forced labor necessarily began to appear both inappropriate and counterproductive to employers*.

Honestly, the textual support for Eltis saying that there was support for abolition ****at all levels**** of society is very thin. There's definitely not a great line reference, but the gist of his explanation is that the capitalists and employers and British leaders (and obviously the slaves themselves) were in favor of abolition.

The passage suggests that Eltis would agree there was "broad-based support" for abolition (across all levels), but would just say the reason for the support was economic.

choices.text: the motives behind Britain’s abolition of slavery were primarily economic
choices.explanation: Eltis agrees with this, but Drescher was providing the more balanced view, and most of paragraph 2 is really stressing the moral / humanitarian explanation for abolition.

choices.text: the moral vision of abolitionists played a vital part in Britain’s abolition of slavery
choices.explanation:
In fact, the second sentence of the 2nd paragraph says, "****Rejecting**** interpretations based on ... moral vision of abolitionists, Drescher ..."

So even Drescher, who was more inclined to think that slavery was abolished for some important non-economic reasons is still rejecting this answer.

choices.text: British traditions of liberty have been idealized by historians
choices.explanation:
The phrase "idealization of liberty" is used at the beginning of the last paragraph.

Eltis thinks that Drescher was idealizing liberty, but Drescher doesn't think he's doing that.

choices.text: Britain’s tradition of political activism was primarily responsible for Britain’s abolition of slavery
choices.explanation:
This is the counterpoint to (B). Whereas (B) expressed Eltis's main hypothesis about abolition, this answer sounds more like Drescher's view.

Eltis, at the beginning of the last paragraph, eschews (rejects) this overly romantic hypothesis based on British traditions of liberty.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Eltis argues against which one of the following contentions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Do we have any text for what Eltis *argues against*?

We know that Eltis ****eschews**** Drescher's idealization of British traditions of liberty.

He's saying, "Yo, Dresch --- you're saying that British people have this sacred tradition of liberty, and that's why they got rid of slavery? Nah. How would you reconcile that with the fact that they were using *low wages and Draconian (very harsh) vagrancy laws to ensure industriousness of workers?* There were even certain famous people calling for Britain to ****enslave**** the unemployed laborers who roamed the countryside."

Eltis thinks that there was wide acceptance of coerced labor (slavery or something resembling slavery).

Eltis also disagreed with Williams in terms of the specific economic reasons motivating abolition of slavery.

Eltis would disagree with the contention that slavery become economically unpalatable because the colonies had become an impediment to economic progress (through bad soil, lots of debt, and inefficient workers).

He thinks it became economically unpalatable because the capitalists wanted money in the pockets of paid-workers who could buy their luxury goods like sugar, coffee, and tobacco.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: We're probably looking for an answer that sounds like Drescher (Britain got rid of slavery because popular sentiment found coerced labor morally abhorrent) or that sounds like Williams (the economic reasons for getting rid of slavery were that colonies were turning into unprofitable ventures).

choices.text: Popular support for antislavery measures existed in Britain in the early nineteenth century.
choices.explanation:
To disagree with this contention would be for Eltis to argue that, "there was ****zero**** popular support for antislavery measures in the early 1800s".

That's too strong a position for Eltis.

choices.text: In the early nineteenth century, colonies that employed forced labor were still economically viable.
choices.explanation:
Williams thought that colonies that employed forced labor were ****not**** still economically viable, and ****that's**** the economic reason that slavery ended.

Eltis disagrees, thinking that the economic reason was something else. But that suggests that Eltis would actually say, "Oh, pish-posh. The colonies employing slavery were still economically viable. That's not the reason slavery ended."

choices.text: British views concerning personal liberty motivated nineteenth-century British opposition to slavery.
choices.explanation:
This comes from the most explicit line of Eltis ****arguing against**** something.

Eltis ****eschews**** (rejects) Drescher's idealization of traditions of liberty. He does not think that slavery ended because British people had such philosophical attachment to liberty that they couldn't morally take it.

He undermines that story (low wages / vagrancy laws / enslave the unemployed laborers roaming the countryside) and offers an economic reason for opposing slavery in its place.

choices.text: Widespread literacy in Britain contributed to public opposition to slavery in the early nineteenth century.
choices.explanation:
This does sound like something from Drescher's paragraph, and we know that Eltis disagrees with Drescher.

But it's hard to say that Eltis would sign off on the claim that, "Widespread literacy ****had zero effect**** on public opposition to slavery."

choices.text: Antislavery measures proposed by conservative politicians in the early nineteenth century met with little opposition.
choices.explanation:
Eltis never says anything relating to how much opposition antislavery measures did / didn't receive in Parliament.

Conceivably, Eltis would agree that antislavery measures passed relatively easily. He would disagree with other people as to the cause of that, but they all fundamentally accept that abolishing slavery did suddenly become something with political will behind it.
